newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower in US after overseas rally fades.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower in US after overseas rally fades.

text.p: The dollar fell broadly on Thursday after an overseas rally against the Japanese yen fizzled and U.S. manufacturing data cast doubt over a Federal Reserve rate hike at the next May 20 meeting, dealers said.

The dollar rallied to a 56-month peak of 127.47 yen in Tokyo before heavy selling by Japanese exporters and life insurers and unconfirmed rumors of looming Bank of Japan intervention brought the rally to a halt.
The dollar closed at 1.7220/25 marks, down from 1.7253/58 at the open and 126.55/60 yen from 126.99/04. Traders said business was thin as much of Europe was closed for May Day.

"A lot of the short-term and interbank traders were expecting a decent run-up once we broke above 127.15/30 yen and the fact of the matter is it didn't go much higher and the Japanese were heavy sellers," said David Gilmore, a partner at market consulting firm Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"That has taken the wind out of the dollar's sails."
Dragging the dollar down further in U.S. trading was the release of the April National Association of Purchasing Management index, which fell to 54.2 from 55.0.

The data suggested a slight slowdown in manufacturing output and reinforced the notion of a strong U.S. economy devoid of worrisome inflation, which was supported earlier this week by gross domestic product and labor cost data.

"Over the last couple of sessions, we've had numbers come out which suggested that perhaps the inflation component of the U.S. economy is not as high as the market had feared," said Audrey McNiff, a vice president in foreign exchange sales at Goldman Sachs.
"This led the market to believe that the potential for interest rate rises is less than expected...and it has taken some of the steam out of the dollar's movement."
Also, a 33-point slide to 6,976 in the Dow Jones industrials average counterbalanced Wednesday's rally over the 7,000 level and dampened dollar enthusiasm.
Supporting the U.S. unit, along with Treasury bonds, was speculation President Bill Clinton and Congress were close to finalizing a balanced-budget accord.
Speaking to reporters at the White House Thursday morning, Clinton hinted that the outlines of an agreement were taking shape.

Later, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton was encouraged by progress in balanced-budget talks but that there was no deal yet. He added that talks may continue on Thursday night and could go into Friday.

Traders said a balanced-budget pact would support U.S. asset markets and ultimately be good for the dollar even though it would most likely entail lower interest rates due to mandatory fiscal tightening and less debt issuance.
The dollar fell sharply against its Canadian counterpart, which rose in celebration of the diminished prospects for a U.S. rate hike at the Fed's May 20 meeting.

The Bank of Canada intervened twice in an attempt to stem the rally by purchasing greenbacks at C$1.3885 and then C$1.3870. The dollar closed more than a cent lower at C$1.3871/76 from C$1.3975/80 at Wednesday's close and below the C$1.3948/53 open.
As Britons raced to the polls in the nation's parliamentary elections, the pound stood nearly unchanged, in contrast to Wednesday's steep slide on pre-election jitters.
Sterling was nearly flat, closing at $1.6235/45 compared to $1.6233/43 at the open. In other trading, the dollar was nearly unchanged at 1.4695/05 Swiss francs from 1.4700/05.
